A Word without a Twin

The translator preparing a new edition of a travel diary faced a difficulty that had little to do ____1____ grammar. The writer repeatedly used one local word for a form of gathering that included food, music and the settling of small disputes. No single English word seemed to cover ____2____ the activities equally well.

At first, the translator chose “festival”. The term was familiar, but it encouraged readers to imagine an event devoted entirely to entertainment. She then considered leaving the local word untranslated. That would preserve its visible difference, ____3____ the risk of making an ordinary social occasion sound mysterious.

A discussion with the editor led to a less dramatic solution. They retained the local term on its first appearance and followed it with a short description. Later references could then use the same word without repeating the explanation. This did not remove every difficulty. It did, ____4____, give readers enough information to follow the diary without pretending that an exact equivalent existed.

The translator also checked ____5____ the term appeared in dialogue or in the writer's later commentary. A gloss that sounded reasonable in a note might be awkward in somebody's spoken sentence. She adjusted the placement of explanations accordingly, while leaving the events themselves ____6____ they were described in the original.

By the time the edition was ready, she had abandoned the idea that a good translation should draw attention ____7____ every choice it involved. Some decisions could remain unobtrusive. Others needed a brief acknowledgement, particularly when an apparently simple English word would otherwise lead the reader ____8____ a different kind of event.

The Work behind the Lines

An exhibition about the history of weather forecasting included several hand-drawn charts. Their ____1____ (ATTRACT) lay partly in their colours, but the curator wanted visitors to notice the practical work behind them. Each line represented a decision about how separate observations should be brought together.

The introductory label warned against treating an old chart as a simple ____2____ (PREDICT) of everything that happened afterwards. Forecasters worked with incomplete information, and some measurements reached them too late to be used. The ____3____ (AVAILABLE) of reports depended on transport and communication as well as on the weather itself.

A second label explained the difference between a chart's ____4____ (APPEAR) and its purpose. A neat line might look certain, even when the evidence beneath it was less ____5____ (CONCLUDE). The museum displayed rough notes beside one finished chart so that visitors could see where a confident-looking boundary had come from.

For the school sessions, the educator prepared a small ____6____ (SELECT) of copies that pupils could handle. She asked them to compare the copies before reading the labels. This encouraged close ____7____ (OBSERVE) without requiring specialist knowledge. It also made the later explanation more ____8____ (MEANING), because the pupils had already noticed something they wanted to understand.

originalGroup.material:
The Green Lunchbox

Milo left his green lunchbox on a bus on Monday morning. At school, he wanted to phone the bus company at once. His teacher helped him read the company's notice first.

The notice said that drivers checked the buses at the end of each route. Small items were taken to the company's office after the last journey, not to the town's main lost-property desk. People could report a missing item online during the day, but collection began at ten the following morning.

Milo filled in the report. He wrote the bus number, the time of his journey and a description of the lunchbox. He also mentioned the small yellow star on its lid. On Tuesday, an office worker phoned his mother. Two green lunchboxes had been found, but only one had a yellow star.

Milo and his mother went to the company's office after school. They showed the report number before the worker brought out the box. The sandwiches were thrown away, but the box was washed and used again. Milo added his name inside the lid. Next time, somebody who found it would have one more way to identify its owner.

Your First Orchestra Rehearsal

Joining a community orchestra can feel daunting if you have only played alone. In your first message, say which instrument you play and how much experience you have. ____1____ Some groups can lend an instrument or suggest a suitable part, so it is worth asking before spending money.

At home, you can prepare without attempting the whole concert programme. ____2____ The word “comfortably” matters: preparation should help you listen and follow, rather than make you struggle with every note.

Break a difficult passage into manageable sections. ____3____ Once a section is secure, add the next few bars. Experienced players also use slow practice when they meet something unfamiliar.

Bring a pencil to rehearsals. You may want to circle an entrance, mark a breath or note a change agreed by the group. ____4____ You should still be able to erase them when the arrangement changes.

Finally, arrive early for your first session. This gives you time to unpack and find your seat. ____5____ Nobody needs to interrupt a piece to work out where an unexpected newcomer should sit. Being prepared is not just about playing more notes; it helps you take part in the group's shared work.

The Pen and the Letter

Last month, an old fountain pen ____1____ (GIVE) to me by my uncle. It had once ____2____ (BELONG) to his father. My uncle had kept it in a small wooden box. When I opened ____3____ box, I found a letter beneath the pen.

The writing in the letter was much thinner ____4____ I had expected. I wanted to try the pen, but my uncle suggested checking it first. Instead ____5____ pressing hard on the page, I was advised ____6____ (HOLD) it lightly and let the ink flow.

A repairer cleaned it before I used it. To my ____7____ (SURPRISE), the pen then moved ____8____ (SMOOTH) across ordinary paper. The repairer explained that I did not need expensive paper for every short note, although some papers would feel different.

I read the letter again. It described a journey ____9____ my uncle had made when he was young. I had already heard the main events, but seeing his own words gave them another voice. I decided that the letter was worth ____10____ (KEEP) with the pen, rather than putting it in a separate drawer.

originalGroup.material:
Giving a Poem Time

A poem on a page offers clues to a reader, but those clues do not all serve the same purpose. Do not assume that the end of every printed line completes a thought. ____1____ A comma or full stop may be more useful than the line ending when deciding where to breathe.

Next, ask who is speaking. ____2____ A line that moves from a remembered conversation to the present narrator may need a different tone even if its words are simple. Read enough of the poem to understand that movement before deciding how a single line should sound.

Try a first reading without aiming at perfection. If possible, record it. ____3____ On the second attempt, change one small feature, such as the place of a pause, while keeping the rest similar.

To examine that pause, repeat the short passage with it and without it. ____4____ The question is what the pause makes clear or holds back. Longer is not automatically better, and a quiet moment need not be empty.

When reading with other people, allow them to finish a thought and give them time to listen to yours. ____5____ A shared reading works best when people can follow the developing meaning rather than race through a fixed number of sounds. Different poems, and different passages within one poem, may ask for different paces.

The Tile a Week Later

The first time I visited a pottery studio, a group of small tiles ____1____ (LIE) on a table near the window. They had been made the day before and were drying slowly. I expected the painted colours to remain exactly the same after firing.

The potter showed me two pieces ____2____ had received the same glaze. One had been fired at a different temperature. Their final ____3____ (APPEAR) was surprisingly different. She explained that colour depended on several parts of the process, not simply on the shade in the wet glaze.

I decorated a tile of my own. Before ____4____ (PUT) it aside, I wrote a small mark on the back so that I could recognise it later. The tile was left ____5____ (DRY) fully before it went into the kiln.

When I returned the following week, it was ____6____ (SMALL) than my original drawing. The potter explained that the material had changed during drying and firing. I was fascinated ____7____ the way a plain-looking surface could become bright and glassy.

The visit required more ____8____ (PATIENT) than I had expected. I could not take a finished object away on the first day. But examining it ____9____ (CAREFUL) a week later gave me time to connect the result with the steps I remembered. We wrapped our tiles ____10____ (WE), using the paper the studio provided.

originalGroup.material:
Reading a Review as an Argument

A book review may tell you whether a critic recommends a novel, but the recommendation is only a beginning. ____1____ A reader seeking a fast-moving mystery may want something different from a reader interested in experiments with narrative voice. Look for clues about the reviewer's intended audience.

Then separate summary from evaluation. A sentence describing a journey belongs to a summary. A claim that the journey reveals the character's refusal to grow is doing something else. ____2____ You can assess that reading of the story without confusing it with a simple statement that the journey occurs.

Examples need attention too. Words such as “because”, “for instance” and “yet” often indicate how a review is organised. ____3____ A vivid quotation may be memorable, but the critic's reason for including it matters more than its vividness alone.

Even after reconstructing the argument, you may not share the judgement. ____4____ The point of careful reading is not to replace your response with somebody else's, but to understand what you are accepting or questioning.

Finally, return to your own reason for reading. ____5____ You might choose the novel, decide it is not for you, or seek a second review with a different emphasis. In each case, you are using an argument as a resource rather than treating a positive or negative verdict as an instruction.

A Camera without a Lens

Before I attended the photography workshop, I ____1____ (EXPECT) to learn about a camera app. Instead, the instructor gave each of us an empty box. We were going to make a camera with no lens.

She showed us a tiny hole through ____2____ light would enter. Then she turned the box around ____3____ (SHOW) where the image would fall. The photographic paper ____4____ (PLACE) inside before the hole was uncovered, so it could not simply be inspected in daylight.

We took the boxes to a courtyard and pointed them towards a building. The length of the ____5____ (EXPOSE) was important. A dimmer scene usually required a ____6____ (LONG) exposure than a bright one. The instructor helped us choose a starting time rather than promising one setting for every situation.

The lid was closed tightly ____7____ (PREVENT) unwanted light from entering. Later, in the workroom, the ____8____ (DEVELOP) image was dried and mounted beside our notes. My first result was blurred, but it still showed the building's outline.

I left with a photograph and some ____9____ (CERTAIN) about how to improve the next attempt: I did not yet know which change would matter most. That was ____10____ kept the workshop interesting. The simple box had made a process visible that I had usually left to an app.
